A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSFT research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, and retained content can be matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning evaluations, matching ablations, training-dynamics analyses, and generated reasoning examples, including Tables 1–2 and the appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original GFPO, code-generation, model-family, and matching-length experiments.

M1.justification: v3 introduces Global Forking Policy Optimization in Section 2.3: reinforcement learning applies policy gradients only to forking-token positions, using complete generations to compute advantages. This adds a training stage and question-conditioned token sampling for Pass@1. The original SSFT matching loss, algorithms, and graph-based selection alternative remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds execution-based LiveCodeBench v5 evaluation, coding fine-tuning data constructed from Open-Thoughts questions, and RL training data from DAPO-Math-17k and Intellect-2-RL. It evaluates transfer from math to coding and from coding to math. The original s1k, Open-R1, and reasoning-benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces the single-<think> SFT-mixed-distill-32B comparator with SFT-mixed-distill-32B-tags, which assigns distinct tags without replacement. The original comparator remains in the coverage plot. Appendix A.3 additionally evaluates tagged SFT with full-sequence GRPO or GFPO and random-matching SSFT with GFPO, substantially expanding the controls.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a 10-step math RL protocol, sampled-token Pass@1 evaluation, Qwen3-4B and Llama3.1-8B configurations, and a matching-length sweep over 0, 100, 1000, 2500, and 3500 tokens. Coding evaluation executes generated programs against tests. The original SSFT training budgets and main math evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 7 newly tests matching-prefix length against training time and accuracy. Section 4 and Appendices A.3–A.6 add RL controls, robustness across model families and training domains, and bidirectional domain-transfer analyses. The earlier random-matching, 93k-data, training-dynamics, and qualitative reasoning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2 and 5 newly specify averaging 16 generations for coding Pass@1. The existing 32-generation math averages and 11-set Cons@6 reporting remain. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the addition concerns documented generation counts.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial RL, coding, model-family, and matching-length results, including SSFT-GFPO AIME24/25 scores of 64.22/58.80 and code-trained SSFT's LCB score of 52.07. Original SSFT scores of 64.06/58.13 and the 93k results remain unchanged. Table 1 replaces untagged-baseline scores of 55.73/51.56 with tagged-baseline scores of 58.23/51.96, which are different-comparator results, and removes cross-task averages.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 newly asserts matching complexity O(NM/k), with k = Tr/L, whereas v2 discusses truncation efficiency without this formal scaling statement. The matching definitions, Hungarian loss, selection equation, and Algorithms 1–2 remain mathematically equivalent. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion now emphasize SSFT plus GFPO and claim superiority over SFT with GRPO across math reasoning and execution-based coding. v2's headline empirical claims concern SSFT versus SFT. Distributed implementation remains documented but loses its place as a headline contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations attributing RL gains to preserved reasoning modes, interpreting coding gains through a larger search space, and acknowledging difficulties theoretically justifying the selection heuristic. It also qualifies generality through smaller gains on other model families and a coding shortfall for Qwen3-4B. These extend the earlier discussion of matching-induced specialization.

D1.justification: Appendices A.3–A.5 and Table 9 document coding-data construction and GFPO implementation, including four-token tag spans, learning rate, batch size, rollout count, KL coefficient, and hardware. Existing SSFT implementation details and access information remain. Coding RL data size is internally inconsistent: the prose and Table 5 state 1000 questions, while Table 9 states 1280.

R1.justification: Appendix A.7 substantially develops positioning relative to RL-based length control, discussing objectives, token budgets, training-data differences, and complementarity. New references also support GFPO and RLVR discussion. Conversely, v2's Parallel-R1 and multi-paradigm reasoning discussions and several associated citations are removed. The DETR-inspired positioning remains.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion, condenses background and figure-related prose, promotes robustness to a standalone section, and moves implementation material later in the appendix. Much of the original explanatory wording and narrative order remains; the larger expansion primarily adds scientific content. Headers, affiliation text, and acknowledgments are also edited.

P2.justification: v3 removes the opening comparison diagram, compresses the inference illustration, relocates learned-matching diagrams to the appendix, and expands boxplot axes to display full whiskers. It adds the matching-length figure and tables for coding, RL, model families, and hyperparameters. Table 1 replaces its average column with LCB and adds GFPO rows.

improvement.justification: Section 4, Figure 7, and Appendices A.3–A.6 substantially strengthen evidence for generality, matching efficiency, and adaptive token selection through coding execution, domain transfer, additional model families, and RL controls. These address important questions left untested in v2. Stale Table 1 gain statements, conflicting coding scores in Tables 2 and 5, and inconsistent coding RL sample counts weaken reporting precision, but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
